uncited: This method performs cone-beam CT reconstruction by mapping projection weights to volume expansion coefficients using a GPU-accelerated kernel that iterates over projection angles.
It solves the inverse problem of tomographic reconstruction by accumulating contributions from filtered projections into a global memory volume buffer.
Geometric parameters: Source-to-Object Distance ($sod$), Source-to-Detector Distance ($sdd$), voxel size ($voxelSize$), and pixel size ($pixelSize$).
- **Volume Buffer:** A 1D array of size $V = NX \times NX \times NY$ allocated in global memory (`CL_MEM_READ_WRITE`).
- **Projection Buffer:** A 1D array of size $W \times H$ allocated in global memory (`CL_MEM_READ_ONLY | CL_MEM_COPY_HOST_PTR`) for the current projection angle.
Each work-item with global ID $gid$ corresponds to a unique voxel in the volume.
The voxel coordinates $(x, y, z)$ are derived from $gid$.
- **Time Complexity:** $O(P \cdot V)$, where $P$ is the number of projections and $V$ is the number of voxels.
Each voxel is processed once per projection.
The volume buffer is stored in global memory, and one projection buffer is allocated and reused.
- **Performance:** The method is efficient for moderate resolution volumes due to the simplicity of the kernel and lack of complex synchronization.
Not optimized for cache coalescing as effectively as tiled approaches.
- **When to use:** Suitable for prototyping, moderate resolution CT reconstruction, and when implementation simplicity is prioritized over maximum performance.
- **When not to use:** For very large volumes or real-time applications where memory bandwidth is a critical constraint.
This method is part of the GPU-accelerated cone-beam CT reconstruction pipeline described in the `ct-reconstruction-gpu` repository.
It serves as a baseline GPU implementation for backprojection, contrasting with more optimized versions using local memory or image textures.
The approach follows the standard FDK (Feldkamp-Davis-Kress) algorithm structure, where filtered projections are backprojected into a volume.
